papers.what_it_is: A journal-length description of Logic Tensor Networks (LTN), a neurosymbolic framework whose differentiable first-order fuzzy logic (Real Logic) grounds symbols in neural networks, with worked examples in classification, regression, clustering, embedding learning and reasoning.

assertions.value: The authors state that LTN introduces a fully differentiable logical language, called Real Logic, in which the elements of a first-order logic signature are grounded onto data using neural computational graphs and first-order fuzzy logic semantics.
quotes: LTN introduces a fully diﬀerentiable logical language, called Real Logic, whereby the elements of a ﬁrst-order logic signature are grounded onto data using neural computational graphs and ﬁrst-order fuzzy logic semantics.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its framework in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that each task is implemented and illustrated with several simple explanatory examples using TensorFlow 2.
quotes: We implement and illustrate each of the above tasks with several simple explanatory examples using TensorFlow 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own evidence: simple explanatory examples.
assertions.reader_inference: The examples are small illustrations, not benchmarks against competing systems, apart from the digit addition comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results indicate that LTN can be a general and powerful framework for neurosymbolic AI.
quotes: The results indicate that LTN can be a general and powerful framework for neurosymbolic AI.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion from simple illustrative examples.

assertions.value: The authors state that this paper extends the product t-norm configuration of LTN with the generalized mean aggregator and introduces solutions to the vanishing or exploding gradient problems.
quotes: this paper also extends the product t-norm conﬁguration of LTN with the generalized mean aggregator, and it introduces solutions to the vanishing or exploding gradient problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states what it adds.

assertions.value: The paper defines a grounding G that associates a tensor of real numbers to any term of the language and a real number in the interval from 0 to 1 to any formula.
quotes: G associates a tensor of real numbers to any term of L, and a real number in the interval r0, 1s to any formula φ of L.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the grounding in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that in Real Logic a variable is assigned to a sequence of values in its domain, the k examples of x, differently from FOL where a variable is assigned to a single value of the domain of interpretations at a time.
quotes: Diﬀerently from in FOL where a variable is assigned to a single value of the domain
in Real Logic a variable is assigned to a sequence of values in its domain, the k examples of x.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of how a variable is grounded.

assertions.value: The paper defines the grounding of a sequence of terms with n distinct variables as a tensor with n corresponding axes, one for each free variable.
quotes: The grounding of tpx1, . . . , xnq, denoted by Gptpx1, . . . , xnqq, is a tensor with n corresponding axes, one for each free variable, deﬁned as follows:
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 3.

assertions.value: The paper defines the semantics of the connectives by first-order fuzzy logic: conjunction, disjunction, implication and negation are associated, respectively, with a t-norm, a t-conorm, a fuzzy implication and a fuzzy negation.
quotes: The semantics of the connectives is deﬁned according to the semantics of ﬁrst-order fuzzy logic [28].
are associated, respectively, with a t-norm (T ), a t-conorm (S), a fuzzy implication (I) and a fuzzy negation (N ) operation
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of connective semantics.

assertions.value: The paper defines the semantics of the quantifiers by aggregation, using a symmetric and continuous aggregation operator Agg applied to the axes of the quantified variables.
quotes: The semantics of the quantiﬁers (t@, Du) is deﬁned with the use of aggregation.
Let Agg be a symmetric and continuous aggregation operator
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of quantifier semantics.

assertions.value: The paper defines diagonal quantification as quantifying over specific tuples such that the i-th tuple contains the i-th instance of each variable in the argument of Diag, under the assumption that all those variables are grounded onto sequences with the same number of instances.
quotes: quantiﬁes over speciﬁc tuples such that the i-th tuple contains the i-th instance of each of the variables in the argument of Diag
under the assumption that all variables in the argument are grounded onto sequences with the same number of instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of Diag, with its stated assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state that for two variables whose groundings contain 10 instances each, forall over the diagonal produces 10 results, whereas without Diag the expression would be evaluated for all 10 times 10 combinations.
quotes: given two variables x and y whose groundings contain 10 instances of x and y each, the expression @Diagpx, yq ppx, yq produces 10 results such that the i-th result corresponds to the i-th instances of each grounding.
Without Diag, the expression would be evaluated for all 10 ˆ 10 combinations of the elements in Gpxq and Gpyq.
assertions.certainty_reason: Worked count that follows from the definition of Diag.

assertions.value: The paper introduces guarded quantifiers, which aggregate only over the instances of the variables whose grounding satisfies a condition (a mask); they operate over only a subset of the variables when this symbolic knowledge is crisp and available.
quotes: In many situations, one may wish to quantify over a set of elements of a domain whose grounding satisfy some condition.
Guarded quantiﬁers operate over only a subset of the variables, when this symbolic knowledge is crisp and available.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of guarded quantification.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evaluation of which tuple is safe under a guard is purely symbolic and non-differentiable.
quotes: The evaluation of which tuple is safe is purely symbolic and non-diﬀerentiable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own guarded quantifiers.

assertions.value: The authors state that in crisp and traditional FOL a guarded universal sentence and the corresponding universal implication would be equivalent, but in Real Logic they can give different results, and that no gradients are attached to the instances that do not verify the mask.
quotes: In crisp and traditional FOL, the two statements would be equivalent.
they can give diﬀerent results.
there are no gradients attached to the instances that do not verify the mask.
assertions.certainty_reason: Settled by a worked example in Section 2.3 with its conditions stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that the best performing symmetric configuration for the connectives uses the product t-norm for conjunction, its dual t-conorm for disjunction, standard negation, and the Reichenbach implication, a subset called Product Real Logic in the cited work.
quotes: In general, the best performing symmetric conﬁguration7 for the connectives uses the product t-norm TP for conjunction, its dual t-conorm SP for disjunction, standard negation NS, and the Reichenbach implication IR
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors choose the generalized mean ApM with exponent p at least 1 to approximate existential quantification and the generalized mean with respect to the error, ApME, with p at least 1 to approximate universal quantification.
quotes: Appropriate aggregators for D and @ are the generalized mean ApM with p ě 1 to approximate the existential quantiﬁcation, and the generalized mean w.r.t. the error ApME with p ě 1 to approximate the universal quantiﬁcation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the aggregators used.

assertions.value: The authors state that with p of 2, ApME is equivalent to 1 minus the root-mean-square error between the vector of truth-values and a vector of 1's.
quotes: With p “ 2, it is equivalent to 1 ´ RMSEpa, 1q, where RMSE is the root-mean-square error
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The identity follows from the formula of ApME for p of 2, so it is easy to check.

assertions.value: The authors state that Product Real Logic still has gradient problems: the product t-norm and the probabilistic sum have vanishing gradients on the edge cases where both inputs are 0 and both inputs are 1, respectively.
quotes: Nevertheless, Product Real Logic still has the following gradient problems:
gradients on the edge case a “ b “ 0; SP pa, bq has vanishing gradients on the edge case a “ b “ 1;
assertions.certainty_reason: Gradient analysis the paper takes from the cited work and from its Appendix C.

assertions.value: The authors define two projections, pi0 and pi1, with an arbitrarily small positive real number, and derive from them the stable operators of the Stable Product Real Logic configuration.
quotes: To address these problems, we deﬁne the projections π0 and π1 below with an arbitrarily small
We then derive the following stable operators to produce what we call the Stable Product Real Logic conﬁguration:
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the stable operators.

assertions.value: The authors state that the conjunction operator in stable product semantics is not a t-norm, because it does not satisfy the identity condition: for any a below 1, the stable conjunction of a and 1 differs from a, although the small constant can be chosen arbitrarily small.
quotes: It is important noting that the conjunction operator in stable product semantics is not a T-norm
does not satisfy identity in r0, 1r since for any 0 ď a ă 1,
although can be chosen arbitrarily small.
For example, the conjunction operator in stable product semantics is not a t-norm, as pointed out at the end of Section 2.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the experimental evaluations of the paper they find that the adoption of the stable product semantics is an important practical step to improve the numerical stability of the learning system.
quotes: we ﬁnd that the adoption of the stable product semantics is an important practical step to improve the numerical stability of the learning system.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no ablation without the stable operators is reported in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment compares stable and unstable operators, so the claim has no reported measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that for p equal to 1, ApME corresponds to the arithmetic mean, and that as p increases, for the same input, the value of the universally quantified formula decreases as ApME converges to the min operator.
quotes: If p “ 1 then ApMEpa1, . . . , anq corresponds to the arithmetic mean.
As p increases, given the same input, the value of the universally quantiﬁed formula will decrease as ApME converges to the min operator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the text without a proof.

assertions.value: The paper defines a theory of Real Logic as a triple made of a set K of closed first-order logic formulas defined on the set of symbols, a parametric grounding for all the symbols and logical operators, and a hypothesis space for the parameters of each symbol.
quotes: Deﬁnition 4 (Theory/Knowledge-base). A theory of Real Logic is a triple T “ K, Gp ¨ | θq, Θ , where K is a set of closed ﬁrst-order logic formulas deﬁned on the set of symbols S
is the hypothesis space for each set of parameters θs associated with symbol s.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 4.

assertions.value: The paper defines the satisfiability of a theory with respect to the aggregating operator SatAgg as SatAgg applied to the groundings of the formulas in K.
quotes: Deﬁnition 5. The satisﬁability of a theory T “ K, Gθ with respect to the aggregating operator SatAgg is deﬁned as SatAggφPK Gθpφq.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 5.

assertions.value: The paper defines learning as the process of searching for the set of parameter values that maximize the satisfiability of the theory with respect to a given aggregator.
quotes: learning is the process of searching for the set of parameter values θ˚ that maximize the satisﬁability of T w.r.t. a given aggregator:
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of learning in Section 3.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that learning the grounding of constants corresponds to learning embeddings, learning the grounding of functions to learning generative models or a regression task, and learning the grounding of predicates to a classification task.
quotes: The learning of the grounding of constants corresponds to the learning of embeddings.
The learning of the grounding of functions corresponds to the learning of generative models or a regression task.
Finally, the learning of the grounding of predicates corresponds to a classiﬁcation task in Machine Learning.

assertions.value: The paper defines four types of queries of a grounded theory: truth queries, value queries, generalization truth queries and generalization value queries.
quotes: A ﬁrst type of query is called truth queries.
The second type of query is called value queries.
The third type of query is called generalization truth queries.
The fourth and ﬁnal type of query is generalization value queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitions of the query types.

assertions.value: The paper defines a closed formula as a logical consequence of a knowledge base at threshold q if, for every grounded theory, whenever the satisfiability is at least q the grounding of the formula is at least q.
quotes: Deﬁnition 6. A closed formula φ is a logical consequence of a knowledge-base
if, for every grounded theory K, Gθ , if SatAggpK, Gθq ě q then Gθpφq ě q.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 6.

assertions.value: The authors state that applying the fuzzy logical consequence definition directly to Real Logic is not practical, since in most practical cases the satisfiability of a grounded theory will not equal 1.
quotes: A direct application of this deﬁnition to Real Logic is not practical since in most practical cases the level of satisﬁability of a grounded theory pK, Gθq will not be equal to 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of the classical definition and uses it to motivate the threshold.

assertions.value: The authors define the first reasoning option, querying after learning, as approximate logical inference that considers only the grounded theories that maximally satisfy the knowledge base, and call a formula a brave logical consequence when it reaches the threshold in all of them.
quotes: This is approximate logical inference by considering only the grounded theories that maximally satisfy
We therefore deﬁne that φ is a brave logical consequence of a Real Logic knowledge-base

assertions.value: The authors state that the first reasoning option is somewhat naive: even with multiple optimizations from multiple parameter initializations, the obtained groundings may not be representative of other optimal or close-to-optimal groundings.
quotes: This approach is somewhat naive.
the obtained groundings may not be representative of other optimal or close-to-optimal groundings.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own option 1.

assertions.value: The authors define the second reasoning option, proof by refutation: they search for a counterexample to the logical consequence by introducing an alternative search objective.

assertions.value: The authors state that if a counterexample is found, the logical consequence does not hold, and if no counterexample is found, the logical consequence is assumed to hold true.
